newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU urged to end obstacles to free movement.
newsitem.headline: EU urged to end obstacles to free movement.

text.p: The European Union should take action to make it easier for its citizens to cross borders to work, study or unite their families, an EU advisory group said on Tuesday.

Despite being promised freedom of movement by the EU treaty, many citizens still face obstacles in areas including residence cards, taxes, car registrations, pensions, training certificates and health care, the panel said in a report(*).

The eight-member High Level Panel on Free Movement of People, headed by former French Social Affairs Minister Simone Veil, proposed some new laws but put the emphasis on better information, cooperation between national authorities and enforcement of existing rules.
"We do not have a high level of mobility in the Union," EU Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn told a news conference, saying that made it difficult to build a European labour force.

The group made 80 recommendations, including introduction of a one-year European residence card that could be used by students, trainees, volunteers and artists who move temporarily to other countries.

It said the EU should amend its rules to make it easier for workers who cross borders to be joined by family members, for example non-dependent children over 21 years old and parents -- and possibly also by unmarried partners, it said.

Visa requirements should also be abolished for non-EU nationals who are members of a family of EU citizens, it added. The group otherwise sidestepped the question of free movement for third-country nationals.
The EU needs to address the tax problems of cross-border workers, which are now governed by bilateral accords rather than by EU rules, the panel said.
It said the EU should draw up rules to bar discrimination against non-resident workers, noting that they are often subject to higher taxes than others in their home country.
EU states should also coordinate car registration tax systems to ensure that individuals who move are not subject to more than one set of taxes, it said.
Flynn said that based on the report, he would reintroduce legislation before the summer to guarantee workers the right to take their company pension rights with them when they move across borders.
The initial proposal was derailed last year because of concerns in Germany about how it would affect its national schemes, which aim to reward employees for long service.
The panel said the law should ensure that workers who take a job in another EU state keep pension rights they would have been entitled to if they had moved to a new employer in the irhome state.
The group also asked the EU to step up its efforts to inform citizens of their rights.

EU Internal Market Commissioner Mario Monti said more than 450,000 people had contacted the EU's new "Citizens First" information programme since November with questions about issues such as social security and residence rights. - - - - (*) Report of the High Level Panel on the Free Movement of Persons chaired by Mrs Simone Veil
